analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum patient protections for managed care plans, including emergency care and appeal rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor; it sat in two House subcommittees until the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a set of patient protections into federal law for people enrolled in managed care (HMO-type) health plans. It would have guaranteed coverage of medically necessary care, emergency room visits without prior approval, a choice of providers and specialists, the right to a second opinion, and language assistance for enrollees who need it. It would have banned plans from paying doctors bonuses to limit care, banned contract clauses that stop doctors from telling patients about treatment options, and required a fair appeals process with independent outside review when a plan denies care. It would also have applied these rules to employer health plans governed by the federal ERISA law and let patients sue managed care plans in state court for injuries.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of Americans enrolled in HMOs and other managed care plans, especially people with chronic illnesses, women needing obstetric and gynecological care, patients who speak limited English, and anyone whose plan has denied or delayed treatment. The bill would have given them enforceable rights to necessary care, easier access to specialists and emergency rooms, and an outside appeal when a plan says no.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Managed care enrollees, especially patients with chronic illness

how_it_helps.text: Plans could not limit or deny covered services that a treating health professional determined were medically necessary and appropriate, and patients could get a covered second opinion [S3].

Emergency room coverage would be required without prior authorization and whether or not the hospital was in the plan's network, using a 'prudent layperson' standard for what counts as an emergency [S3].
Patients would gain a choice of providers and specialists, direct access to an obstetrician-gynecologist, and continuity of treatment if a plan dropped a doctor mid-course-of-treatment [S3].
Plans could not offer doctors financial incentives to reduce medically necessary care, and contract 'gag clauses' restricting what doctors may tell patients would be void [S3].
Denials of care would be subject to grievance procedures and independent external review, with the plan paying the review's costs and barred from retaliating against patients who appeal [S3].

Plans could not discriminate against enrollees or providers based on race, gender, language, age, disability, or health status, and would have to provide trained medical interpreters where 2% of enrollees need language assistance [S3].

The bill would extend these protections to employer group health plans under ERISA, which had previously shielded many plans from state insurance rules, and would let patients bring state-law damage suits against managed care plans for injuries or wrongful death [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance plans and the employers that sponsor them would bear the cost of building adequate provider networks, covering out-of-network emergency and specialty care, paying for external reviews, and defending against state lawsuits. Those costs would likely be passed on partly through higher premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers sponsoring plans

drawbacks.text: The mandates would raise the cost of covering employees: plans would have to cover out-of-network providers (within copay limits), maintain at least one primary care physician per 1,500 enrollees, and pay for external reviews, costs likely passed into premiums [S3].

Section 4 would open managed care plans to state-court damage suits for personal injury or wrongful death; employers and insurers argued this exposure raises premiums and could prompt plans to drop coverage [S3].

Several standards are vague — 'adequate access,' 'reasonable' copays, a Secretary-determined provider mix — which could invite litigation and regulatory disputes over exactly what plans must provide [S3].

The drug provisions bar plans from limiting drug coverage 'solely on the basis of costs' and from setting substitution standards, which would constrain tools plans use to hold down drug spending [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections address real, documented harms of 1990s-era managed care — denials of necessary care, gagged doctors, blocked emergency coverage — and the appeal and external-review machinery is a reasonable check on plan decisions. The honest cost side is substantial: broad out-of-network mandates, strict network rules, and new lawsuit rights would raise premiums, and some small employers might respond by cutting coverage. The bill's design gives regulators wide discretion, which cuts both ways. On balance it is a consumer-protection bill whose main risk is cost rather than harm to patients.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2001, sent to two House committees, then parked in subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Nydia Velazquez introduced the bill on July 12, 2001 [S1][S5].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Education and the Workforce Committees, then in late July and early November 2001 to the Health and Employer-Employee Relations subcommittees respectively [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and no further action of any kind [S4][S5].
Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died in subcommittee without a vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care insurers and employers that sponsor health plans came out ahead: they avoided federal patient-protection mandates, external review costs, and exposure to state damage suits. Patients in managed care plans gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velazquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Managed Care Bill of Rights for Consumers Act of 2001 on July 12, 2001.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in the Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after its November 2001 referral to the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed patients' bill of rights legislation containing broad rights to sue health plans in state court, the same liability provision contained in Section 4 of this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred to reveal a partisan split; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans (HMOs)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed network adequacy, emergency coverage, appeal, and nondiscrimination requirements on managed care plans and let patients sue them in state court for injuries. Plans profiting from denying or delaying care would have lost that ability.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring health plans under ERISA
industries.note: The bill would have extended all the new protections to self-insured employer plans that state insurance law generally cannot reach, adding compliance costs, and expanded liability exposure tied to those plans.
